Second-largest US coal producer files for bankruptcy

Second-largest US coal producer files for bankruptcy

Alpha Natural Resources, America’s biggest producer of metallurgical coal and the country's second-largest coal producer, filed for bankruptcy protection Monday. The bankruptcy filing cited a multi-year fall in demand for coal--in particular, metallurgical coal used for steel production--amid a deepening slump in the global economy.

An Alpha Natural Resources mine in Sylvester, WV

The bankruptcy endangers the jobs of the company's 8,000 workers, most of whom live in Appalachia, a region whose economy has been devastated by decades of coal layoffs.

Alpha is the seventh, and by far the largest, US coal producer to file for bankruptcy over the past year, and there are indications that the move will spark a renewed wave of job cuts in the mining industry.

Alpha CEO Kevin Crutchfield said the main aim of the bankruptcy was to “restructure our debt and protect our operations.” These are euphemisms for ripping up union contracts and slashing jobs to improve the company's profitability in a depressed market. Alpha’s mines will remain in operation for the present thanks to a $692 million financing package arranged by Citigroup.

United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) International President Cecil E. Roberts signaled that the union was prepared to work with the company in imposing concessions demanded by the company's creditors. Roberts declared that the UMWA was “willing to discuss ways forward that will be of mutual benefit for the company and for our members.”

His response is in keeping with the record of the UMWA, which has collaborated in the elimination of nearly 100,000 mining jobs in US since the mid-1980s.

Alpha had lost nearly its entire share value following its 2011 purchase of Massey Energy in the aftermath of the 2010 Upper Big Branch disaster that killed 29 Massey miners.

Hoping to capitalize on the disaster by buying up Massey for a song, the company did not anticipate the subsequent downturn in coal prices and production. Forbes magazine noted, “Alpha Natural Resources has idled or closed more than 80 mines since July 2011, fired 6,500 workers, and cut capital expenditures by 55 percent to $225 million in 2015.”

The bankruptcy filing triggered a renewed sell-off Monday of major US coal producers’ stock. “Regardless of each individual company’s balance sheet, the majority of the space is priced as if investors expect bankruptcies,” one analyst told the Wall Street Journal .

On Tuesday, St. Louis-based Patriot Coal sent at least 1,000 layoff warning notices in preparation for its potential sale to another company, Blackhawk Mining. The possible sale is linked to the company's second bankruptcy over the past decade, which began in May.

Patriot Coal was spun off from its parent company, Peabody Energy, “purposely to fail in order to dump costs associated with retirees who had worked for the two companies,” the UMWA said in a statement. In 2013, during the company's first bankruptcy, a federal judge ruled that the company could slash benefits owed to coal miners and retirees, many of whom suffer debilitating physical ailments such as black lung.

Decades of mass layoffs have left Appalachia's economy devastated. West Virginia has the highest unemployment rate in the United States and is the only state with a workforce participation rate under 50 percent. Nearly one in six of the state’s working-age adults receives disability benefits, according to Labor Department data.

Since June 2014, 2,900 West Virginia miners have lost their jobs, while some 4,300 construction workers and 2,200 people working in leisure and hospitality have been laid off over the same period.

In announcing the bankruptcy filing, Crutchfield predicted the failure of more US coal companies. “The US coal industry as currently structured is unsustainable,” he said, adding, “challenges the US coal industry has experienced over the last several years are greater than any in the past three decades.”

He pointed to “macroeconomic headwinds” including “rapidly falling coal prices” due to, among other causes, “slower than expected economic growth in both the United States and overseas markets” such as Europe and China. He added that coal prices have reached a ten-year low this summer.

Pointing to [these charts], he noted that “prices for met coal [used in steel production] and thermal coal [used for energy production] have respectively fallen by approximately 72 percent and 44 percent since 2011, and central Appalachian coal production has declined by approximately 50 percent since 2008 and by approximately 37 percent since 2011.”

The renewed attack on coal miners is part of a wave of mass layoffs in oil and other extractive industries. Oil companies have carried out over 50,000 job cuts over the past three months as oil prices have continued their slump. Oil is currently trading at under $50 per barrel despite producers’ hopes that its price would increase in the second half of this year.

Oil consulting firm Swift Worldwide Resources reported in June that over 150,000 jobs have been lost globally since the beginning of the downturn in oil prices last year. These losses have been centered in the United States and the North Sea. Swift CEO Tobias Read noted that his firm’s estimate of 150,000 is actually “conservative and the likelihood is that total job losses probably exceed Swift’s forecast.”

Last week, multinational oil giant Royal Dutch Shell announced that it would eliminate 6,500 positions this year. These moves were accompanied by an announcement that Shell was planning to proceed with a takeover of BG Group, a step that will likely result in further layoffs.

This followed the announcement by British-based mining conglomerate Anglo American, the world’s fifth largest mining company, that it would cut 53,000 jobs in the coming period.

The collapse in the prices of commodities used heavily in industrial production, including coal, oil and iron ore, points to the depressed state of the real economy on a world scale despite six years of soaring stock markets. Last month, the International Monetary Fund predicted that this year would record the lowest global growth rate since 2009.

What makes a good video game story?

Storyless games can be good, but I think that a good story line is important especially in single player game modes. As for what makes a good story, I'm not a writer at all, but my favorite stories are the ones that take me to another world and make me forget that I'm playing a game. Where I feel anticipation for the characters because I feel like I'm one of them. I think that atmosphere plays a large role in that, but pacing is important too. I don't want things to move so quickly and with so many new characters that I lose motivation for remembering their names. Games that move me along too slowly let me get sidetracked and I forget about the story while I'm doing other meaningless tasks. I think that the story itself has to feel important, to get me to care about the outcome and the characters. This is all from the perspective of a player and not a creator, but these are the things I appreciate in a good story line.

Characters. Definitely the most important aspect is characters. Lovable, dynamic characters. Understandable characters. Characters ment to be hated yet still dynamic and do good at times. The truth of the matter is, there's no true formula to success. Different people like different things. So the key, really, is to know your audience and present people, choices and events that they are interested in.

One thing that can be learned though, is pacing. Don't be afraid to have a cool down period after something large and dramatic. A lot of games do that via use of an overworld, or cutscenes. But it can be anything that brings a pause. The most important part is to remember that you don't have to constantly rush into a new, big, bombastic set piece. And you do not have to constantly make everything bigger and better

the real question is "what makes a good story?" a story is a story, whether it's told via a film or a video game, a book or a song.

regarding your first question, the answers are going to vary from person to person, but IMO: a story needs to have strong characters, well-written dialogue etc. the fundamentals are what counts the most here. I'm looking for things like motivations, character development and arcs, things like that.

regarding your second question, you can absolutely make a good game without a story, or with a minimal story element. you see, for everything a good story can add to a game experience, a bad, poorly-written, or hamfisted story will take just as much away.

A story that can only be told in an interactive medium and not in a film or book. Otherwise, it might be a good story and can be evaluated as that, but can't be considered a good story for a video game.

Examples of stories that only work well in a video game: Stories with alternative branches such as Mass Effect or Witcher.

Examples of stories that work best in video games: Stories with optional branches such as Skirym.

Examples of stories that only work because they are told in a video game: Braid.

Neither of those categories imply good or bad but rather what to consider in the first place before you evaluate as good. There is much more to say about this, but I consider this the essentials.

Guy working in game dev here, I'll try to answer the best I can.

First of all: if you want into the game dev industry and you feel that ideas are your strong suit, your best bet is to learn both writing and game design.

How do you make a good/interesting story? What makes a story interesting or good? What makes someone want to continue with a story, or get involved in it? As a gamer, what does a game do to keep you engaged with its story?

The short answer is, the same way you produce anything else that's good. Make sure the ingredients going into your story are good. Your setting is going to be incredibly important, because the player experiences it first-hand. Fill it with immersive details, interesting ideas, and populate it with memorable characters. Your players should be able to empathize with the characters, and gain an interest in discovering their motivations. You mention the idea of the underdog, which is something that's quite easy to relate to. Look at the game from the point of view of your expected typical player, and ask yourself what else might resonate strongly with them.

Do you think story is the crux of gaming/media, on which everything else hangs, or can you have a successful/really good game with a weak or stupid story?

I think you answer this question yourself. A story is a game-enhancing thing, like music or graphics. This is why I recommend you take an interest in game design; good game play is the foundation upon which everything else is built. Game play will make players invested in the game, which in turn will make them want to be further invested in the story.

Hope that helps!

Personally, I prefer games that let you inhabit the story instead of telling you. From first hand experience I consider games like Portal, Half-Life 2 and from what I hear Dark Souls to be among the best of this.

Half-Life 2 especially doesn't really tell you a story, but has you inhabiting it. They don't have some character brief you on why there is a resistance movement. You just hear the refugees talking, crying, alluding to what's happened to them as you imagine people naturally would. G-Man never shows up and goes "HELLO! I'M FROM THE INTERDIMENSIONAL RESISTANCE MOVEMENT INHABITING A HUMAN FORM AND SUPPORTING YOUR EARTH STRUGGLE" He just is sort of always in the background, and clearly more than human. The same thing goes for the nature of the combine troops, and what's happening at the prison, etc, etc.

What I love about these things is you can engage with them as much as you want. Do you want to walk around soaking up the story through osmosis, letting enough of the atmosphere cling to you until a cogent notion of the situation forms? Or do you want to just blast on ahead with your most immediate objectives? This is especially nice on repeated playthroughs.

What is also most evident is that this form of storytelling is hard. Which is why so few games do it. You need an incredibly well fleshed out game world, and you need to think about how that world would naturally hang together. What are the rules of this world? How do those rules motivate people to act? How would it influence their art and culture? What sorts of conflicts would naturally emerge? How would the different forces of this world naturally try to one up each other?

Now don't tell the player any of that! Just show them the outcomes of all those forces acting on the game world. And maybe, if you're lucky, a few dedicated fans will publish rarely seen fan theory videos and validate all the effort you put into the story.

When the story progresses with the player rather than around the player, it also really helps when gameplay doesn't suffer for the sake of ramming the story down your thought (Max Payne3 comes to mind because who ever was responsible for that is probably in the wrong career, they should be in the movie business not video games)

Deux Ex Human Revolution has a nasty habit of progressing the story while youre off crawling though vents and reading emails. Almost every time Jensen ventures out to do some vital mission he returns to find some new story development has happened in his absence, by the end I wasn't remotely interested in any of the choices at the final section.

Dishonored does something similar to Human Revolution, I wasn't interested in any of the characters in Dishonored but at least the gameplay made up for it. By the end I didn't care who I killed or who I let live.

Ghostbusters: The Video Game is a good example of a well made story in a game, dialogue is interesting, characters have charm and more depth than your usual over the shoulder run and gun game. Closest thing to a 3rd Ghostbusters movie we will ever get.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is another very good example of a game with a good story, it does get a bit cliche at times and the villain is a bit over the top but the protagonist and his allies tell an interesting story without trying to make the gameplay take a back seat at any point.

It really comes down to personal preferences, I'm sure someone loved Max Payne 3 for the very reasons I hate it.

You can definitely have a game succeed if it has stupid ass story. Halo didn't have a great story. It wasn't bad, but it was pretty simple. But it was an amazing game because of all the innovations it did, and the graphics, and the atmosphere, and the combat. However, good story will make a game that much better. It's something video game designers have to stop looking past. Good writing is important. It will help a game succeed. It motivates the player.

From playing DnD, watching animes and playing video games, I feel like there are two effective types of stories: Immature, over the top, big explosions and impossibilities, and mature, small scale, struggling for life.

Minor plot twists that makes everything tied together are important. Witcher 3 pulls this off amazingly well. It makes the world feel alive, and not just some pathway to make you the hero.

Also, having a solid and relatable reason to save people is very important. FF7 kinda failed at this part, with your characters just being ordinary people involved in an extraordinary scheme, and they just HAPPENED to be there. Accidentally saving the world just feels like a cop-out, and it's one of the major complaints I have for FF7.

For some inspiration on storyline: Planescape: Torment (often considered the best RPG ever made for its story). Bastion and Transistor (dark games with colorful, living worlds, made by the same company). Valkyrie Profile: Covenant of the Plume (Plays like Fire Emblem, but you KNOW that you are playing the villain throughout the entire game, pulls it off very well).
